title: Impatience Can Be About People or Outcomes
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article dissects a subtle but consequential distinction in how leaders express impatience: whether it targets people or targets outcomes. The author explains that when impatient leaders ask 'why' something is late or hasn't happened, they inadvertently blame the people involved, breeding defensiveness and resentment. Reframing that same impatience as 'what' is in the way, and shifting from 'you' to 'we,' redirects the pressure toward solving the problem collaboratively rather than assigning fault. The piece closes with a quote from Macy's CEO Tony Spring to illustrate how a small ingredient, or a small shift in language, can make an outsized difference.
points: Impatience directed at people breeds defensiveness; impatience directed at outcomes invites collaboration.
Asking 'why' something is late implicitly blames the person responsible.
Reframing questions from 'why' to 'what' shifts focus toward removing obstacles together.
Shifting language from 'you' to 'we' makes impatience feel like a shared push rather than an accusation.
Small shifts in how impatience is expressed can dramatically change team responsiveness.
quotes: Great leaders often fight an internal war against their own impatience.
The direct or indirect blame aimed at them pierces like a knife of contempt.
Impatience can be about outcomes or about people. The best leaders always make it about the outcomes.
Statements of Why express dissatisfaction with the people involved.
Going from Why to What and from You to We makes impatience more palatable and drives the point home in positive and reinforcing manner.
As Macy’s CEO Tony Spring likes to remind people, “It doesn’t take a lot of baking powder to make bread but without it, you don’t have bread.
